prompt: Explain the Senate filibuster using only baseball rain-delay metaphors. Do not stop when the metaphor stops working.

In the grand stadium of democracy, passing a bill is just trying to play a standard nine-inning game of baseball. But sometimes, the minority team realizes they are going to lose if the final out is recorded. So, they deploy the ultimate tactic: they stare up at a perfectly clear blue sky, feel a single phantom drop of moisture, and signal the grounds crew to drag the giant, heavy canvas rain tarp across the entire infield. 

This is the filibuster. As long as the tarp covers the diamond, the game cannot end, the score cannot be finalized, and no one can swing a bat. 

In the old days of the sport, a player actually had to stand barefoot in the mud, holding the edge of the tarp while reading the Doppler radar out loud until their voice went hoarse. They had to physically prove it was raining, talking about barometric pressure and dew points for twenty-four hours straight. If they dropped the tarp or sat down in the dugout to eat sunflower seeds, the umpires would shout "Play ball!" and the legislation would pass. 

But modern rules have created the "silent rain delay." Today’s players don’t even need to touch the canvas. A manager simply sends an email to the commissioner threatening to look at a cloud, and the tarp magically covers the infield. Even weirder, because the tarp is covering the main diamond, the two teams will just wander over to the bullpen and play a completely different, unrelated exhibition game (like confirming a minor-league postmaster) while the main game remains indefinitely suspended under the tarp.

This rule mandates that exactly 60 out of the 100 people in the stadium must march onto the field in unison, grab the brass handles of the tarp, and heave it off the grass. It doesn’t matter if 59 people are pulling with all their might; if they don't have that 60th person, the tarp stays, the rain delay stretches into legislative eternity, and the stadium hot dogs rot in the concession stands.

Once a season, the players are allowed to pretend the rain delay isn't happening, provided they are arguing about team payroll. If they touch the plate beneath the tarp, the game counts.
